programmeBriefingSlides.title:
Welcome to Information Technology:
Systems Development
programmeBriefingSlides.subtitle: FETC · SAQA 78965 · NQF Level 4 · 165 Credits · 15 Days · 3 Blocks
programmeBriefingSlides.speakerNote:
Welcome everyone. Before we open any unit content, we spend a few minutes orienting: what this qualification is, what you will be able to do by the end, and why it matters for your learners and your professional practice.

Ensure attendance registers are signed and PoE folders are distributed now — this session is short and we want full attention once we begin.

Tone to set: energetic and forward-looking. This is not a compliance exercise — it is the opening of a 15-day journey that changes how these lecturers teach systems thinking.

Keep this brief — 2 minutes maximum. Mention your background in both software development and systems analysis. The credibility point matters: learners need to see that this content is grounded in real professional practice, not just academic theory.

Optional: share one real project you have worked on that required both analysis and development skills. One sentence is enough. It anchors your authority early.

programmeBriefingSlides.title: What is Information Technology?
programmeBriefingSlides.subtitle: The invisible infrastructure every organisation depends on
bullets: IT is the combination of hardware and software products and services that organisations use to manage, access, communicate, and share information
IT is not just computers — it underpins every business function
Force 1 — Changes in the world: globalisation, remote work
Force 2 — Changes in technology: cloud computing, AI
Force 3 — Changes in client demand: systems must be faster
programmeBriefingSlides.highlight: As systems developers, learners will design, build and maintain the IT infrastructure organisations depend on. Understanding WHAT IT is — and WHY it must be planned — is the foundation of every unit in this qualification.
programmeBriefingSlides.speakerNote:
Ask: 'Name one IT system your institution runs on that would cause serious disruption if it went down for a full day.' student records, payroll, logistics, service delivery Use the answer to anchor the three forces — the system they named exists because of Force 1, runs on technology shaped by Force 2, and must meet expectations driven by Force 3.

Stress that IT planning is not a technical problem — it is a business problem. The three forces create the pressure. Systems development is the discipline that responds to that pressure in a controlled, professional way.

Keep this to 4 minutes. Do not go into technical depth on any of the three forces — that is Unit content. This slide creates motivation and context, not instruction.

programmeBriefingSlides.title: What is a System?
programmeBriefingSlides.subtitle: A vocabulary frame — we will apply this properly in Unit 1
bullets: A system is an organised set of interrelated components working together toward a defined goal
An information system collects, processes, stores and distributes data to support operations and decisions
Every information system follows one structural pattern: Input → Process → Storage → Output
Example: a student registration portal captures enrolment data, checks eligibility, generates student numbers, and updates timetables
programmeBriefingSlides.highlight: Four words to carry into Unit 1: Components · Input/Output · Processes · Feedback. These are your analytical vocabulary — not content to memorise here, but a framework you will apply all day in Session 1.
programmeBriefingSlides.speakerNote:
This slide introduces vocabulary — it does NOT teach system analysis. That is Unit 1's job.

Say explicitly: 'I am not going deep on this now. I want you to have four words in your head before we open Unit 1. We will apply them properly once we are in the unit.'

Ask one quick question only: 'Name one IT system you interact with at CET every day. What does it take in? What does it produce?' Take two answers maximum. Do not analyse them — just acknowledge and move on.

Forward pointer — say this clearly: 'In about 20 minutes, when we open Unit 1: Information Systems Analysis, we will go deep on what systems analysis actually means as a professional discipline. What you are doing now is getting the vocabulary ready so that depth lands faster.'

Do NOT explain the four dimensions (Components, Input/Output, Processes, Feedback) in detail here. Briefing-level is: name them, give one example sentence each. The full analytical treatment belongs in Unit 1 Slide 6 and the pre-session slides.

programmeBriefingSlides.title: What is Systems Development?
programmeBriefingSlides.subtitle: 6 phases — coding is only phase 4
bullets: Investigation — Identify and confirm the business problem
Analysis — Establish exactly WHAT the system must do
Design — Specify HOW it will work: architecture, data structures, module structure, user interfaces
Development — Write and unit-test the code
Implementation — Deploy, manage the transition to live operation
Maintenance — Monitor for defects, fixes and plan future iterations
programmeBriefingSlides.highlight: Coding (phase 4) only appears more than halfway through. Analysis and design before it determine whether what gets built is actually useful. A technically perfect system that solves the wrong problem is still a failure.
programmeBriefingSlides.speakerNote:
Read the phase list left to right — one sentence each. Keep it fast .: requirements, data flows, user needs, constraints; based on the approved design documents;  convert existing data, train users; .The point is NOT to teach the SDLC here — it is to show learners that development is a structured discipline with phases, not just 'write code until it works'.

The punchline is the highlight: phase 4 (code) comes after analysis and design. Most people think systems development IS coding. Correct that misconception now, gently.

Forward pointer — say explicitly: 'Unit 1 opens with this lifecycle in detail. By the time you finish Session 1 today, you will be able to describe each phase, name its deliverable, and explain what happens when it is skipped. Right now I just need you to see the shape.'

Do NOT teach feasibility, requirements analysis, or the SDLC in depth here. This slide creates the overview. Unit 1 delivers the substance.

programmeBriefingSlides.title: Systems Development vs Software Development
programmeBriefingSlides.subtitle: Different scopes — deeply connected
bullets: Software Development —: design, write, test, and deploy software artefacts
Systems Development —: people, process, data, technology AND code
Software development is a SUBSET that sits inside systems development
The analyst determines WHAT to build and WHY · The developer determines HOW to build it
In this qualification: you will think like an analyst AND write like a developer
programmeBriefingSlides.speakerNote:
Clear up the most common misconception before learners carry it into the unit content: this is NOT a pure coding course.

Frame the expectation plainly: 'Roughly 40% of this programme is analysis and design thinking. 60% is implementation. Both halves make you a complete professional. If you only know how to code but cannot analyse a problem, you will build the wrong solution. If you can only analyse but not build, you cannot deliver anything.'

The WHAT/HOW distinction here is introduced at motivation level. Unit 1 Slide 17 operationalises it — teaching learners HOW to establish WHAT through requirements analysis tools and techniques. Do not go there now.

Keep to 3 minutes.

programmeBriefingSlides.title: Why Does This Qualification Matter?
programmeBriefingSlides.subtitle: Four reasons anchored in South African IT
bullets: Organisations run on systems — every business function depends on reliable information systems that someone designed and built
Poor analysis = expensive failures — most IT project failures trace to misunderstood requirements, not bad code (Standish CHAOS Report)
NQF Level 4 opens careers — analyst, developer, BA support and project coordination roles are in demand across SA government and industry
Professional practice modelling — structured thinking (analyse → design → build) is the standard the workplace expects and the standard you will model for your learners
programmeBriefingSlides.speakerNote:
This is the motivational anchor of the entire briefing. Pause here and let it land.

Ask: 'Who here has experienced an IT system that did not do what was expected — one that was built, delivered, and then rejected or rebuilt?' Wait for a show of hands or a verbal response. Then: 'That is the problem this qualification trains you — and your learners — to prevent.'

The Standish CHAOS Report statistic (more than 70% of IT project failures trace to poor requirements) will come up again in Unit 1. Plant it here as a seed: 'We will come back to this number in Unit 1. By the end of today you will understand exactly why requirements analysis is where most projects are won or lost.'

programmeBriefingSlides.title: Your 10-Module Roadmap
programmeBriefingSlides.subtitle: 15 days · 3 blocks · 56 credits delivered
bullets: Block 1 · Days 1–5 · Foundations (23 credits): Systems Analysis (today), Team Collaboration, Programming Principles, Problem Solving, Design
Block 2 · Days 6–9 · Applied Programming (14 credits): Apply Programming Principles, Web Scripting
Block 3 · Days 11–13 · Systems in Practice (19 credits): Testing IT Systems, Resolve User Problems, Work as Project Team Member
Each unit ends with a formative quiz (self-check) and an assessment task for your Portfolio of Evidence
programmeBriefingSlides.highlight: 56 credits delivered across these 15 days. Remaining credits toward the full 165-credit qualification are achieved through workplace evidence in your PoE.
programmeBriefingSlides.speakerNote:
Distribute the printed module roadmap now if available. Run through the colour-coded block overview — 90 seconds maximum. The goal is for learners to see the sequencing logic: foundations first, applied programming second, systems in practice third.

Point to today specifically: 'We start right now with Unit 1 — Information Systems Analysis. Everything else in this programme builds on what you learn today. If the analysis foundation is clear, every subsequent unit lands easier.'

If learners ask about specific blocks or units in detail, defer: 'We will brief each unit as we arrive at it. Right now let us focus on getting Unit 1 started.'

programmeBriefingSlides.title: Ready to Begin
programmeBriefingSlides.subtitle: Briefing complete — Unit 1 opens now
bullets: ✓  You know what Information Technology is and the three forces shaping it
✓  You have the vocabulary frame for systems: components, input/output, processes, feedback
✓  You can name the 6 phases of Systems Development and why coding is only phase 4
✓  You understand the distinction between systems development and software development
✓  You know your 10-module roadmap across 3 blocks
✓  You know how to reach your facilitator between sessions
programmeBriefingSlides.speakerNote:
Pause for genuine Q&A — 3 to 5 minutes maximum. Answer only orientation questions here. Any content question ('what exactly is a DFD?', 'how does Agile work?') gets deferred: 'That is a great question — and exactly what Unit 1 covers. Let us get into it.'

Then navigate to Unit 1 and open with the title slide.

Handoff line to say clearly: 'The briefing gave you the map. Unit 1 gives you the first destination in depth. Everything we named in the briefing — systems, lifecycle, analysis vs development — we are now going to examine properly. Let us begin.'
